title: HE CHOSE THE BETTER LAND.
paragraphs: HE CHOSE THE BETTER LAND.

Green fields.
Shimmering rivers.
Endless opportunity.

Short-term gain.
Long-term regret.
Brother, lean in.
In Book of Genesis 13, a quiet decision becomes a generational disaster.
Abram and Lot stand on a ridge. The land can’t hold both their flocks. Strife is rising. So Abram—father in faith—offers his nephew first choice.
Grace gave Lot the microphone.
And Lot lifted his eyes.
He saw the Jordan Valley — “well watered everywhere… like the garden of the Lord” (Genesis 13:10).
It looked like Eden.
But it was leaning toward Sodom.
The text whispers something chilling:
“Lot chose for himself…”
For himself.

Not “What honors God?”
Not “What protects my family?”
Not “What preserves righteousness?”
Just — what prospers me.
The grass was greener.
So he moved closer.
Closer.
Closer.
Verse 12 says he pitched his tents near Sodom.
Not in it.
Near it.

Compromise rarely begins with a headline sin.
It begins with proximity.

You don’t fall overnight.
You drift.

And the next chapter? War.
The next chapters? Wickedness.
By Genesis 19, Lot is inside Sodom, sitting at the gate — a civic leader in a corrupt city.

Short-term gain.
Long-term grief.

Some scholars interpret Lot as a believer whose soul was “tormented” by Sodom’s sin (see 2 Peter 2:7–8). If so, hear this: even the redeemed can live in self-inflicted misery when they prioritize prosperity over presence.
Lot got the valley.
Abram got the promise.
After Lot separated, God told Abram:
“Lift up your eyes…” (Genesis 13:14)
Notice the contrast.

Lot lifted his eyes to see land.
Abram lifted his eyes to hear God.

One chose by sight.
The other walked by faith.
And here is the scandal of grace:

Abram, the wronged one, becomes the blessed one.
Lot, the chooser, becomes the captive.
Sin always overpromises.
It sparkles like the Jordan at sunrise — cool blue waters, golden light dancing on the surface — but beneath it is a current pulling you toward Sodom.
Brother. Sister.
Where have you pitched your tent?

Near what?
Close to what?
Flirting with what?
The Gospel does not shame you. It calls you home.
Jesus Christ did not choose the “better land.” He chose the cross.

He stepped into our Sodom.
He absorbed our compromise.
He bore the fire meant for us.
On that hill called Calvary, He reversed Lot’s story.

Where we chose for ourselves,
He chose to save.

Where we drifted toward sin,
He moved toward us in mercy.
Repentance is not losing land.
It is gaining life.

Turn the tent.
Move away from Sodom.
Lift your eyes again — not to the valley, but to the Savior.
Because in Christ, even compromised believers can be restored.
This is not the end of your story.
